This is part six of a series on statistical methods for infectious disease epidemiology, with a focus on time-to-event, or "survival", data.



In this post I'll describe two statistical inference methods (non-parametric and parametric multi-state survival models) and the conditions under which these multi-state methods can be used to investigate intermittently-observed data.

## Aalen-Johansen estimator {#aalen-johansen}

The non-parametric Aalen-Johansen estimator can be used to estimate the transition probability matrix, $\mathbf{P}(t)$ for a Markov process with a finite number of states. Firstly, let $\mathbf{A}(t)$ be the matrix of cumulative transition intensities from state $r$ to state $s$:

$$
\mathbf{A}(t) = A_{r,s}(t) =
\begin{cases}
\int_{0}^{t}{q_{r,s}(u) du} & \text{if } r\neq s \\
-\sum_{s \neq r}{A_{r,s}(t)} & \text{if } r = s
\end{cases}
$$

The transition probability matrix for this process can be represented as the (time-ordered) matrix product:

$$
\mathbf{P}(t) = \prod_{k = 1}^{K}{\left(\mathbb{I}+\Delta\mathbf{A}(t_k)\right)}
$$

where $t_1 < \ldots < t_K \leq t$ are the times at which transitions take place, $\mathbb{I}$ is the identity matrix, $\Delta\mathbf{A}(t_k) = \mathbf{A}(t_k) - \mathbf{A}(t_k \mbox{-})$, and $t_k \mbox{-}$ represents the instant before time $t_k$. Substituting the Nelson-Aalen estimator for $\mathbf{A}(t)$, then the Aalen-Johansen estimate of the transition probability matrix is:

$$
\mathbf{{\hat{P}}}(t) = \hat{P}_{r,s}(t) = \prod_{k =
1}^{K}{\left(\mathbb{I}_{r,s}+\Delta\hat{A}_{r,s}(t_k)\right)}
$$

with:

$$
\Delta\hat{A}_{r,s}(t_k) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{\Delta N_{r,s}(t_k)}{Y_{r}(t_k \mbox{-})} & \text{if } r\neq s \\
\frac{-\Delta N_{s}(t_k)}{Y_{s}(t_k \mbox{-})} & \text{if } r = s
\end{cases}
$$

where $\Delta N_{r,s}(t_k)$ is the number of transitions from state $r$ to state $s$ at time $t_k$, $\Delta N_{s}(t_k)$ is the number of transitions away from state $s$ at time $t_k$, and $Y_{r}(t_k \mbox{-})$ is the number of individuals in state $r$ just before time $t_k$.

The Aalen-Johansen estimator requires the times of transitions between states to be observed exactly (together with the state occupied by each individual at all times). It is therefore not directly applicable to intermittently-observed data, where the times of transitions are interval-censored; this is the main motivation for the likelihood-based approach described below.

## Multi-state mixture models {#multi-state-mixture-models}

For a general multi-state competing risks mixture model, assume that an individual $i$ who begins in state $r$ makes a transition to a (pre-assigned) destination state $s$. Let $I_{i,r}$ be the indicator variable which determines which transition will occur, the transition intensity at time $t$ is:

$$
q_{i,r,s}(t) =
\begin{cases}
q^{*}_{i,r,s}(t) & \text{if } I_{i,r} = s \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

where $q^{*}_{i,r,s}(t)$ is the transition intensity for the transition which occurs. The probability of transition to state $s$ is defined as:

$$
\begin{align*}
\pi_{r,s} & = \Pr(I_{i,r} = s)
\end{align*}
$$

Let $T_{r,s}$ be the the time from entering state $r$ to moving to state $s$, given that this transition occurs (i.e. the conditional sojourn time). A parametric distribution with parameters $\theta_{r,s}$ and conditional density $f_{r,s}(. \mid \theta_{r,s})$ may be used to model $T_{r,s}$.

### Transition probabilities {#transition-probabilities}

The probabilities of competing events $\pi_{r,s}$ can be related to a set of $m$ covariates $\boldsymbol{z} = \{z_1, \ldots, z_m\}$ via multinomial logistic regression. Define as $S_r$ the set of all competing states after $r$, then the logit of transition to a given state $j \in S_r$ vs.\ transition to a baseline state $0 \in S_r$ is:

$$
\ln\left(\frac{\pi_{r,j}(\boldsymbol{z})}{\pi_{r,0}(\boldsymbol{z})}\right) = \alpha_{r,j} +
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{r,j}^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{z}
$$

with $\alpha_{r,j}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{r,j} = \{\beta_{r,j,k};\; k = 1, \ldots m\}$ being regression coefficients for the probability of transition to state $j$.

Meanwhile, parameters $\theta_{r,s}$ of the time to transition distribution can be related to a different (or identical) set of $l$ covariates $\boldsymbol{x} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_l\}$ via a log-linear model (for parameters which are constrained to be positive) with coefficients $\gamma_{r,s}$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{r,s} = \{\omega_{r,s,k};\; k = 1, \ldots, l\}$:

$$
\log(\theta_{r,s}(\boldsymbol{x}))=\gamma_{r,s} + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{r,s}^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{x}
$$

For most parametric time to transition distributions `accelerated failure time' models are considered, where the covariates affect the rate of progression of time, i.e. the survival function $S(t \mid \boldsymbol{x})$ for an individual at time $t$ with covariates $\boldsymbol{x}$ is related to the baseline survival $S^{(0)}$ via:

$$ 
S(t\mid \boldsymbol{x}) = S^{(0)}\left(\exp(\boldsymbol{\eta}^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{x})t\right) 
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ is a vector of regression coefficients.

### Likelihood contributions {#likelihood-contributions}

The likelihood contributions are as follows:

- For an individual who enters state $r$ and reaches state $s \in S_r$ at time $t$: 
$$
l = \pi_{r,s} f_{r,s}(t)
$$

- For an individual who is censored in state $r$ at time $t$:
  $$
  l_c = \sum_{s \in S_r}\pi_{r,s}(1-F_{r,s}(t))
  $$

  where $F_{r,s}(t) = \int_0^t f_{r,s}(x)dx$ is the conditional cumulative distribution of the time to transition from state $r$ to state $s$, given that this transition occurs.

## Accounting for censoring {#accounting-for-censoring}

As described in [part III of this series](/blog/classical-survival-methods/index.qmd#likelihood-estimation), survival models may be specified to account for censoring and truncation in observed data by careful consideration and construction of the likelihood function. Multi-state survival models, in particular, are well-suited to investigating interval-censored, or *intermittently-observed* data.

In the interval censoring figure from [part II of this series](/blog/survival-analysis/index.qmd#interval-censoring), changes in an underlying process were detected with an intermittent observation scheme. Depending on the nature of the underlying process, less frequent and/or irregular observation may result in transitions being undetected, as shown in @fig-intermittent-observation below. This could be an issue for survival models, particularly when there is a dependency between the observation times and the underlying process.

An observation scheme is said to be *non-informative* if the likelihood is proportional to a scenario where observation times were fixed in advance and chosen independently of the underlying process. For example, a study with clinic visits scheduled every four weeks regardless of symptoms is closer to non-informative than a study where extra visits are triggered by clinical deterioration. With a non-informative observation scheme then multi-state models can correctly account for intermittently-observed data.

For a Markov multi-state model, the likelihood for intermittently-observed data only requires the states occupied at the observation times. An individual $i$ observed in states $s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_J$ at times $t_0, t_1, \ldots, t_J$ contributes the product of the transition probabilities between successive observations, regardless of any unobserved transitions in between:

$$
l_i = \prod_{j=1}^{J} P_{s_{j-1}, s_j}(t_{j-1}, t_j)
$$

where, for a time-homogeneous model, $\mathbf{P}(t_{j-1}, t_j) = \exp\left((t_j - t_{j-1})\mathbf{Q}\right)$ as described in [part V of this series](/blog/multi-state-models/index.qmd).

## Implementing multi-state models {#implementing-multi-state-models}

A number of sophisticated statistical software packages exist to implement frequentist and Bayesian survival and multi-state models using the `R` programming language. Frequentist maximum likelihood estimation tends to be less computationally intensive than Bayesian inference, and the latter may require integrating over a vast number of parameters, which is usually impracticable for higher dimensions. Instead, algorithms which simulate from the posterior distribution are often used to evaluate features of these integrals. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms have been widely used for this application.

There are several specialised modelling packages available to fit multi-state models, including: [`survival`](https://github.com/therneau/survival), [`msm`](https://chjackson.github.io/msm/), [`mstate`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mstate), [`etm`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=etm) and [`flexsurv`](https://chjackson.github.io/flexsurv/index.html) which fit models using maximum likelihood or non-parametric estimators, and [`JAGS`](https://mcmc-jags.sourceforge.io/) and [`Stan`](https://mc-stan.org/) which fit Bayesian models using MCMC.

For HIV back-calculation specifically, the [`cd4backcalc`](https://pkirwan.github.io/cd4backcalc/) package implements Bayesian, discrete-time, multi-state CD4-staged back-calculation models in Stan.

Two useful online tutorials for running statistical inference for survival and multi-state models are:

- [Survival analysis in R](https://www.emilyzabor.com/survival-analysis-in-r.html) by Emily C. Zabor

- [Multi-state modelling with msm: a practical course](https://chjackson.github.io/msm/msmcourse/) by Christopher Jackson

::: {.callout-note}
## Key takeaways

- The Aalen-Johansen estimator extends the Kaplan-Meier approach to provide non-parametric estimates of transition probabilities in multi-state models, provided that transitions are observed exactly.
- Multi-state mixture models allow for different transition types with their own probability distributions and covariate effects.
- Intermittently-observed data with interval censoring can be properly handled by likelihood-based multi-state models when observation schemes are non-informative.
- Covariates can influence both the probability of transitions between states and the timing of those transitions.
- Both frequentist (maximum likelihood) and Bayesian (MCMC) approaches are available for fitting multi-state models, with several specialised `R` packages providing implementation.

:::
